reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: getting a vaccination shot at the doctor's office
story:
Owen sat in the waiting room. He held his teddy bear tight. "Your turn," said the nurse. Owen took a big step into the small room. Dad gave him a hug first. The nurse said, "This is quick." Owen looked at his teddy. Then he felt a tiny pinch in his arm. "All done!" said the nurse. "That was fast," said Owen. He got a nice bandage with a star on it.

In the car, Owen rubbed his arm. "It feels sore," he said. "Will it stay sore?" he asked. Dad said, "The spot where you got a shot can feel sore for a little while. It will feel better soon." Owen nodded. He held his teddy's paw.

At home, Owen played with his blocks. He built a tall tower. Then he looked at his arm. The star bandage was still there. He touched it softly. "Not sore now," he said. He smiled at Dad. "Want a hug?" asked Dad. "Yes," said Owen. He ran over fast.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: basic time concepts such as yesterday, today, tomorrow, now and later
story:
Lena woke up in her bedroom. Today was the day. Mom had said, "Today we go to the store." Yesterday they had not gone. Yesterday it rained. Tomorrow would be too late, because tomorrow the store would be closed.

"Now?" Lena asked. "Can we go now?" Mom was still brushing her hair. "Not yet," said Mom. "We go later."

Lena did not like later. Later felt very long. She asked again. "Now?" Then the clock on her bedroom wall made its loud tick sound. Mom pointed to it. "Look," she said. "The clock shows what time it is." Lena looked at the little hands. "When the short hand points to the nine, then we go," said Mom.

Lena watched the clock. Tick, tick, tick. The short hand moved a tiny bit. She got dressed while she watched. She put on her shoes. She found her red hat. She watched some more. Then the short hand was at the nine. "It is nine!" she shouted. "It is time now!" Mom laughed and took her hand.

At the store, Lena picked out apples. She put them in the bag all by herself. "Thank you," she said to the man at the counter. Mom smiled. "We can come back tomorrow too," said Mom. Lena held up the apples. "When the clock says it is time," she said.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: weather words such as sunny, rainy, windy and snowy and the clothes that go with them
story:
Athena put on her warm coat. She put on her red boots. It was snowy at the park. The snow was white and soft. "Snowy day, snowy day!" said Athena. She scooped up a big snowball. "I want to keep it forever," she said. Grandma said, "Put it in your pocket, then." Athena held the cold snowball tight.

At home, Athena took out her snowball. She set it in a glass. "Now I will look at it every day," she said. She went to draw a picture. The sun came out. It was sunny in the window.

Later, Athena came back. She looked in the glass. "Oh no!" she cried. "My snowball is gone. Now it is just water." The warm room had melted it. Snow melts into water where it is warm. "Don't worry," said Grandma. "We can make a new one. And we can grow a paper snowball that stays." Athena smiled. "Snowy day, snowy day," she said, and hugged Grandma tight.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: the rote number words from one to ten heard in counting songs and everyday counting
story:
Aubrey sat at the dinner table. She had ten peas on her plate. She wanted to count them all by herself.

"One, two," she said. Then she stopped. "Oh no," she said. "I forgot what comes next." Her lip wobbled and she looked upset.

Mom smiled. "Sing your shoe song," she said. "The one from the car."

Aubrey sang. "One, two, buckle my shoe. Three, four, shut the door." She peeked at her plate. "Five, six, pick up sticks. Seven, eight, lay them straight." She pushed a pea with her spoon. "Nine, ten, a big fat hen!"

"Look, Mom! I counted to ten!" said Aubrey. "The song helped me remember."

"Yes it did," said Mom. "Now let's count your carrots."

Aubrey pointed at the carrots. "One, two, buckle my shoe," she sang. Dad tapped his spoon to the beat. Aubrey giggled and kept going, all the way to ten again.

After dinner, they drew a big hen. Mom drew a river by the hen. Aubrey drew ten little sticks beside it.

"One, two, buckle my shoe," she sang, and added one more stick.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: to recognise the letters of the alphabet and the sound each letter makes
story:
Charlie sat in her reading nook. She had a soft pillow and a big book. The book was full of letters. Charlie pointed at a curvy letter. "What is that one?" she asked.

"That is S," said Dad. "S says sss." Charlie made the sound too. "Sss," she said. "Sss like a snake!" Dad smiled and nodded.

Charlie went on a hunt. She wanted more sss things. She found her sock. "Sock starts with S!" she said. She found a small bag of sand. "Sand starts with S too!" Then she saw sun light on the rug. "Sun! Sss!" Charlie laughed. "Sun, sock and sand. All S!" She hugged the book like a feather had landed on her. "Stinky socks," Dad said with a giggle. Charlie giggled too. "Sss!" she said.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: going on a family trip away from home
story:
Ava packed her little red bag. She was going to the beach with Mommy and Daddy. Grandma waved from her door. "Bring me a shell!" she said.

The car drove a long, long way. Ava watched trees go by. Then her tummy felt funny. "I need the potty," she said. Daddy said, "We can stop soon. There is a place ahead." Ava asked, "What place?" Mommy said, "A rest stop." The car turned in. Ava held Mommy's hand and used the potty. Then she stretched her arms up high. "Look how tall!" she said.

Back in the car, the drive felt short now. Soon Ava saw blue water. A white boat did float on the waves. Ava ran to the sand with Daddy. She found a pink shell. "This one is for Grandma," she said.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: getting a first library card and borrowing a book
story:
Ivy went to the library with Dad. She got her very first library card. It had her name on it. She picked a big book about a worm. The worm was long and wiggly. "I want to keep this book forever," Ivy said.

The librarian stamped a paper. "This book goes back on your due date," she said. "That is the day it has to come back." Dad read the paper. "Your due date is Saturday," he said. Ivy held the book tight. "But I love the worm book." Dad said, "You can love it, and then bring it back."

At home, Ivy read the worm book three times. She read it to her teddy bear. She read it in her dry, sunny window seat. Saturday came. Ivy put the book in her bag. She carried it to the desk all by herself. Then she saw the shelf. "Can I take this one now?" she asked. The librarian smiled and stamped a new paper. "A new due date," she said. Ivy hugged the new book. "See you on Saturday," she told the worm book on the shelf.

activity: learning to swim at the local pool
story:
Raphael stood in the pool changing room with his dad. His swim shorts had a tight waist. Dad helped pull them up. "Swim time!" said Raphael. He ran to the door.

Dad caught his hand. "Walk, please. Wet floors are slippery," said Dad. "So we walk near the pool." Raphael looked down. The floor was shiny and wet. It even smelled like pool water. He tried one big step. His foot slid a little. Whoops!

"I see it," said Raphael. "Wet floor, slippery feet!" He walked slowly, one step at a time. His feet stayed under him. At the door, a small surprise waited. His friend Mia was there, holding a rubber duck. "Want to play a walking game?" she asked. "Who walks slowest wins?" Raphael laughed and walked with her all the way to the pool.

activity: to recognise the letters of the alphabet and the sound each letter makes
story:
Sofia sat at the big table. She had paper and crayons. Her mom had a bag of letter cards. Sofia pulled one out. "S," she said. "S makes the sss sound, like a snake."

Mom smiled. "Now find S somewhere in the house." Sofia looked and looked. She stopped at her lunch box. There was her name on it. S-o-f-i-a. "There is my S!" she said.

"Write your name," said Mom. Sofia wrote it slowly. She made a small s first. It looked little and shy next to the other letters. Mom wrote Sofia's name on her own paper. Mom's S was big and tall. "Your S is a capital letter," Mom said. "A name starts with a big one." Sofia looked at her small s. Then she looked at Mom's big one.

Sofia rubbed out her small s. She drew a big capital S. She sat back and looked at her name. It stood up tall. "Sofia," she read out loud. "S makes sss. And my S is the big one." She held the paper up to the window so the sun could see it too.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: learning to swim at the local pool
story:
Aaron stood in the pool changing room. He pulled on his swim shorts all by himself. Then he sat on the bench and looked at his toes. "Will the water be too big for me?" he asked. Dad smiled. "The teacher will be there," he said. "Her name is Miss Jo."

The pool room was huge and bright. Blue water made wavy lights on the wall, like someone used paint to draw them. Aaron held Dad's hand tight. Miss Jo said, "Time to float on your back." Aaron shook his head. "I will sink!" Miss Jo put her hands under his back. Her hands held him up, just like that. He did not sink. He lay on the water and looked at the ceiling.

"I'm floating!" Aaron called. Then a small surprise came. A splash of water jumped up and made the wall light wiggle. Aaron laughed. Dad waved from the side. "Can we come again tomorrow?" Aaron asked. Miss Jo said, "Yes, we sure can."

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: weather words such as sunny, rainy, windy and snowy and the clothes that go with them
story:
Liam looked out the window. The sky was gray. Big drops fell on the glass.

"Is it rainy today?" Liam asked.

"Yes," said Mom. "Rainy and windy. See the tree move?"

The tree bent and swayed. The leaves shook.

Liam put on his boots. He put on his coat. Mom took the umbrella. It was red with yellow dots.

They walked to the car. The rain went tap, tap, tap. Mom held the umbrella over both of them.

Liam put out his hand. His hand stayed dry. The rain hit the umbrella instead.

"The umbrella keeps the rain off my head," Liam said.

"It does," said Mom. "It keeps mine dry too."

At school, Liam looked at the snow pictures on the wall. "Snow is cold," he said. "I wear my mittens in snow."

Mom smiled. "One day it will snow. Then we will wear hats and mittens."

Liam drank his juice from his cup. He sat up straight for story time.

"When will it be sunny again?" he asked.

"Soon," said Mom. "Then we wear our sun hats."

Liam waved. "Bye, Mom. Stay dry!"

Mom opened the red umbrella and walked home through the rain.

activity: pretend play scenarios such as playing house, caring for toys and role-playing simple situations
story:
Sara ran to the little orange kitchen at the playground. "Time to make soup!" she said. She stirred leaves and pebbles in a pot. Her bear sat in a chair with a bib on. "One spoon for you, bear," said Sara. "Two spoons for baby doll. Three spoons for me." The soup smelled like leaves and sunshine.

Then Ben came over. "Can I play house too?" he asked. "You can be the dad," said Sara. Ben fed the bear a pebble pie. They laughed and made a big mess. Cups were everywhere. Leaves were on the floor.

Then Sara's mom called, "Time to go home!" Sara looked around. "Our pretend game is done," said Ben. "So the toys get put away." Sara picked up the cups. Ben put the pebbles in a bag. One, two, three, four cups. The bear went in the stroller. The kitchen was clean again. "Goodbye, little house!" said Sara. She waved at the orange pot all the way to the gate.

activity: the idea that printed words carry meaning and that books are read front to back
story:
Emilia went to the library. She wanted her favorite book. It had a bear on the cover. Emilia looked on the shelf. She found books about cats. She found books about trucks. No bear book. Her feet tapped the floor. She wanted to kick a little, but she took a big breath instead.

The librarian knelt down. "Tell me the book's name," she said. "The name on the front is called the title." Emilia looked at a cover. There were little words there. "The words say the name?" she asked. The librarian nodded. "Yes. The words mean something."

Emilia found the bear book. The title said Bear Gets Sleepy. She opened the front cover first. She turned the pages, one by one, all the way to the back. "I read the words," she said. The librarian smiled. "You found your book." Emilia hugged it tight. "Bear Gets Sleepy," she read. "That is its name."

activity: pretend play scenarios such as playing house, caring for toys and role-playing simple situations
story:
Amelia ran to the play kitchen at daycare. It was soup day! She wanted to make the best soup ever. Her friend Leo was already there, holding a big plastic pot.

"Let's make soup!" said Amelia. She put in a pinecone, a leaf and two round play dough balls. Then she stirred with a long wooden spoon. The soup smelled like nothing at all, but that was okay. It was pretend soup.

Amelia lifted the spoon to her mouth. She wanted to taste it. "Stop!" said Miss Kim, the teacher, coming over fast. "Pretend food is for pretending to eat." Amelia looked at the spoon. Oh! She held it near her lips and made a big slurping sound. "Sluuurp!"

Leo peeked into the pot with wide eyes. "More soup please!" he said, holding out his arm. Amelia ladled out a pretend scoop. Leo pretended to slurp too. "Yum!" he said. They both laughed and clapped.

Then Teddy the bear got a pretend bowl. Amelia fed him one tiny pretend bite. "Good job, Teddy," she said. Miss Kim gave them both a thumbs up, and Amelia stirred the pot again, faster and faster, because soup day was the best day ever.

activity: opposite pairs such as big and small, hot and cold, fast and slow
story:
Clara got to school and saw the snow. Big snowflakes fell. They fell fast, then they fell slow. Clara wanted to play outside. But her scarf was too short. The cold wind got in. "Brrr," said Clara.

Her friend Mia had a very long scarf. It wrapped twice around her neck. Mia said, "Mine is long. Yours is short. Long and short are opposites." Clara touched Mia's long scarf. It was soft and warm. Her own scarf felt small in her hand.

The teacher, Miss Pam, came to help. She found a big box of yarn. Clara picked red yarn. Miss Pam helped her sew. Clara worked slow and careful. First it was short. Then it got longer. Then it was very long. "I did it!" said Clara.

Outside, the snow squeaked under her boots. Clara's new scarf wrapped twice, just like Mia's. A naughty snowball flew by. It was Tom, playing a joke. Clara laughed. Then she helped sweep snow off the slide, fast, fast, fast. The slide shined. "My turn!" she called.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: basic color words such as red, blue, yellow and green
story:
Lucy wanted to draw the snow. She got her doll to watch. She looked in her crayon box. "I see red, yellow, green," she said. "But where is the sky color?"

She held up a dark blue crayon. "Is this blue? It looks so dark."

Her brother Ben grabbed a pale one. "No, this one is blue. Yours is not."

Lucy lined up the crayons on the table. Light blue. Middle blue. Dark blue, like the deep night sky. "One, two, three blues!" she said.

Ben picked up the dark one. "It is blue too," he said. "Dark blue and light blue. Both are called blue."

Lucy smiled. She drew soft white snow. She drew a light blue sky up high. She drew dark blue water down low.

"Two blues, one picture," said Lucy. Her doll got a blue hat too.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: learning to play a musical instrument
story:
Logan had a violin. It was small and shiny. He wanted to play a song for his cat.

Mom held out a long stick. "This is the bow," she said. Logan grabbed the bow. He held it the wrong way. He poked the violin with the fat end.

"Squeak!" went the violin. The cat ran under the chair. Logan made a sad face. "That was a bad sound," he said. "This is hard."

Mom sat close to him. She turned the bow in his hand. "Now pull it across the strings," she said. "Slow and smooth."

Logan pulled the bow across the strings. The violin sang. It made a long, pretty note. Logan pulled again. Another sweet note filled the room.

The cat came out from under the chair. It sat down near Logan. Its tail swished to the music.

Logan played one more note. The cat purred. Mom clapped her hands. "Play it again," she said.

Logan laughed and pulled the bow across the strings one more time.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: going to the dentist for the first time
story:
Aurora was three. Today she went to the dentist for the first time. In the waiting room there was a big fish tank and a chair that spun like a wheel. A young boy sat next to her. He held a blue toothbrush. Aurora held her green one.

The nurse said, "You can both show me how you brush." Aurora put down her green toothbrush. Then she picked up a toothbrush to brush. But it was the blue one! The boy laughed. "That is mine!" he said.

Aurora looked at the blue brush. Then she looked at the green one on the chair. She put the blue one in his hand. She took her green one back. Each person had their own toothbrush now.

The nurse said, "Ready, Aurora?" Aurora hopped up onto the big chair. It spun her around, whee, like a wheel. She opened her mouth wide and brushed her big toy teeth with her green toothbrush.

"Did I do it right?" she asked.

"Yes!" said the boy, and he clapped.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: basic time concepts such as yesterday, today, tomorrow, now and later
story:
Isabella ran to the rug at school. "Story now!" she said.

Miss Kim smiled. "Not now, Isabella. Now means this very moment. The story is after snack."

Isabella looked at the clock. The big hand was not at snack yet. So she waited. First she ate her apple. Then she drank her milk. Then the clock showed snack was done.

"Now?" she asked.

"Now!" said Miss Kim. She opened the big book up high so all could see.

Isabella clapped. "Yesterday we had the bear story," she said. "Today we have the dog story!"

"That's right," said Miss Kim. "And tomorrow you can pick the book."

Isabella looked at her friend Leo. "Tomorrow I will pick the dinosaur book," she told him.

"After school, I will tell my mom at dinner," said Leo.

Isabella sat up tall. She had waited, and the story came.

Miss Kim turned the first page. "Once there was a little brown dog," she read.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: cooking or baking a meal for the family
story:
Leon was at Grandma's house. Snowy flakes fell outside the window. Today Leon would help make bread.

Grandma let him pour the flour. She added water. Leon mixed it with a spoon. Then he touched it with his hands. The dough stuck to his fingers. It felt gooey and lumpy.

"Oh no," said Leon. "The bread is ruined. It is all sticky."

Grandma laughed softly. "It is not ruined," she said. "Watch me." She pushed the dough with her hands. Then she folded it over. Push and fold. Push and fold.

"Can I try?" asked Leon.

"Yes," said Grandma. "This is how cooks do it."

Leon pushed the dough. He folded it over. The sticky bits came off his hands. The dough turned smooth and soft. It made a funny squishy noise.

Grandma put the bread in the oven. Leon stood far back, because the oven was hot. Soon the kitchen smelled warm and good.

"Grandma," said Leon, "did I make this?"

"You did," said Grandma. She cut a slice. Leon took a big warm bite.

"Mmm," said Leon. "Push and fold!"

activity: to throw a beanbag into a hoop and catch a large ball with both hands
story:
Gabriel went to the park with his dad. The sun was warm. Ducks sat by the pond and fish in the water. Gabriel had a red beanbag and a big blue ball.

There was a hoop on the grass. Gabriel wanted to throw the beanbag in. He tossed it. It hit the rim and fell out. He tried again, slower. The beanbag went in. "I did it!" said Gabriel.

Then his little friend Mia came to play. Gabriel threw the big ball to her. He threw it hard and fast. It flew past her hands and bumped her arm. Mia sat down on the grass.

"Oops," said Gabriel. He picked up the ball. He walked closer. He tossed it slow and soft. Mia held out both hands. The ball landed right in them. She laughed. "Again!" she said. Gabriel smiled and gave the ball a gentle toss.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: the rote number words from one to ten heard in counting songs and everyday counting
story:
Wyatt wanted to zoom his rocket ship. He had a small red rocket made of paper. But the rocket would not fly. It just sat on the rug.

Dad sat down next to him. "Rockets need a countdown," Dad said. "Counting backward from ten down to one is called a countdown." Wyatt patted the soft rug. He was ready to try.

"Ten, nine, eight," said Wyatt. A little bug crawled by. "Seven, six, five," he said. His tummy felt jumpy like jelly. "Four, three, two, one." He took a big breath. "Blast off!" Wyatt jumped up high. He threw the rocket into the air. It zoomed over the couch and landed on the rug. "Again!" said Wyatt. Dad laughed and held up ten fingers. "Ten," said Wyatt, and he started the countdown once more.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: simple object categories such as animals, toys and foods
story:
Elizabeth had a big box of blocks. She wanted to make a rainbow on her floor.

First she picked all the red blocks. Then she picked all the blue ones. Soon she had a red pile and a blue pile and a yellow pile. "Look, Mommy!" she said. "The colors go together!"

Then her big brother Sam came in. He sat down with her. He picked up a red block, a blue block, and a yellow block. "These are all little," he said. He put them in one pile. Then he found a red one, a blue one, and a yellow one that were all big. He put those in another pile.

Elizabeth blinked. "But the colors are all mixed!" she said. Sam laughed, gently. "You sorted by color. I sorted by size."

Elizabeth tried it too. She found all the little blocks and stacked them. Then she found all the big blocks. Her tower grew tall. But there were also square blocks and round blocks. "Those are square," she said. "Those are round."

Mommy came to look. "You sorted them three ways," she said. "Colors, sizes, and shapes." She gave Elizabeth a kiss on her head.

Outside, a truck rumbled down the street. Elizabeth waved at it. Then she picked up a round block and set it on top of her tower. It stayed. "Big round one," she said.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: learning to play a musical instrument
story:
Alexander sat on the little red chair. The music room had drums, a piano, and a big basket of shakers. On the wall hung a small guitar with a pig sticker on it. Alexander wanted to play that guitar.

Miss Rosa took it down for him. "You can play it today," she said. Alexander pulled the strings. Plunk. Plonk. He pulled them again. It sounded funny. It did not sound like the song they sang. Alexander frowned at the pig sticker. "It sounds wrong," he said.

"Let me fix it," said Miss Rosa. She held the guitar and turned the little pegs at the top. Turn, turn, turn. "This is called tuning," she said. Then she pulled a string. Ding. It sounded clear and sweet.

Miss Rosa gave the guitar back. Alexander pulled the strings. Ding. Ding. Ding. He sang their hello song, and the guitar sang too. He tapped his itchy sweater sleeve to the beat. Then he played one more note, very soft, for the pig.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: to name the five senses and say which body part is used for each
story:
Jake wanted to play a game. "I will find all my senses," he said. His mom said, "That is a nice game."

Jake put his hands over his eyes. It was dark. He could not see the sun. He opened his eyes. "I see with my eyes!" he said. "I see the sun and the tree."

Jake found a flower. He sniffed it with his nose. "I smell with my nose," he said. He touched the grass. "I feel with my hands." A bird sang. "I hear with my ears." His mom gave him a berry. Jake ate it. "I taste with my mouth."

Then Jake got dirt on his face. His mom helped him wipe it off. "Five senses," said Jake. He held up five fingers. "Eyes, nose, hands, ears, mouth!"

His mom clapped. "You did it, Jake."

Jake covered his eyes again. "Now I see nothing!" Then he peeked. "Now I see you!"

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: the rote number words from one to ten heard in counting songs and everyday counting
story:
Matthew went to the store with Mama. He held her hand. "Can we buy new socks?" he asked. "Yes," said Mama. "You need a pair."

Matthew looked at the sock shelf. There were red socks and blue socks. He picked up one red sock. "Where is its friend?" he wondered. "A pair means two," said Mama. "Like a pair of socks."

So Matthew looked again. He found the other red sock hiding under a blue one. He put the two socks together. "One, two," he said. "Now it is a pair!" Mama smiled.

The store had a big lamp by the shoe hats. The lamp made a warm glow on the floor. Matthew counted the shoes under it. "One, two, three, four, five," he said. "Can I count more?" "Count them all," said Mama.

They walked past the fruit. "What would you like?" asked Mama. "Apples," said Matthew. He put them in the bag, one at a time. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven." He stopped and looked in the bag. "How many is that?" "Seven," said Mama. Matthew carried the bag to the man at the desk. "Hello," said the man. "Apples for you?" "Seven apples," said Matthew. "And a pair of socks!"

activity: watching a big game with family and friends
story:
Aurora sat on the big clean rug. The whole family was watching the game. Aunt Rosa brought a bag of popcorn. The popcorn was warm and salty.

On the TV, tall players ran fast. One player threw the ball up high. The ball went through the hoop. The crowd cheered loud. "The ball went in the hoop!" said Dad. Everyone clapped and jumped. Aurora clapped too. She wanted to try that.

Aurora found her soft red ball. She looked around the room. She saw the laundry basket on the floor. She stood back a little. She threw the ball up. It hit the rim and fell out. She tried again. This time the ball went through the basket. "I scored!" Aurora said. She stirred her popcorn with her fingers and smiled. Dad gave her a big high five.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: to recognise the letters of the alphabet and the sound each letter makes
story:
Elijah wanted to write his name. He had a sticky marker and some paper. He knew his name started with E. But he could not remember how to make it.

He drew a tall line. He drew some little lines. "That does not look right," he said. Mom came to sit by him.

Mom had a card. The letter E was on it. The E was bumpy, like tiny hills. "You can trace it," Mom said. "Use your finger as a tool." Elijah put his finger on the bumpy E. He went down, down the tall line. Then across, across, across.

The bumps tickled his finger. He giggled. He traced it again. Down, across, across, across.

Then he picked up his marker. He drew a tall line on his paper. Then he drew one line across. Then another. Then one more. He looked at his letter.

"That is E!" he said. He wrote E, l, i, j, a, h. Some letters were wiggly. But the E was just right.

Mom clapped her hands. Elijah traced the bumpy E one more time. "Tickle, tickle," he said, and laughed.

activity: simple object categories such as animals, toys and foods
story:
Ellie went to the library with Mama. She wanted to find the toy box. The librarian said the toys were in the playroom. Ellie walked down the little hall.

A boy named Sam was cleaning up. He held up each toy and said its name. "One block," said Sam. He put it in the toy box. "Two dolls." In they went. "Three balls." Ellie watched the box fill up. Blocks, dolls and balls are all toys, she thought. The toy box got full and full.

Then the box was empty. Sam had put everything away. Ellie wanted a ball to roll. She looked and looked. "Where are the toys?" she asked. Sam pointed to the box. "They are all in there," he said. Ellie opened the lid. There was the red ball on top.

Ellie rolled the ball to Sam. Sam rolled it back. Round and round it went. A sleepy baby watched them from a big pillow in the corner. Soon the room grew quiet. The librarian came to close the playroom door. "Time to rest," she said softly. Ellie hugged the red ball and gave it back to Sam. "One ball," said Sam, and put it in the toy box.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: the idea that printed words carry meaning and that books are read front to back
story:
Ella sat on her bed with a big book. She opened the front cover first. On the first page, she saw little black marks. "What are those?" she asked. Grandpa said, "Those are words. They tell a story." Grandpa read them out loud. Ella listened.

Then Ella wanted to write words too. She got paper and paint. With her brush, she painted letters. She painted them all touching, like a long train. HITHISISELLA. She gave the paper to Grandpa. Grandpa looked and looked. He turned the paper around. "I can't read this yet," he said. Outside the window, the sky was cloudy, so they had lots of time.

Ella looked at her book again. She saw little gaps between the words. "The words have spaces," she said. "Can I try that?" Grandpa nodded. Ella painted her letters again, slowly. This time she put a space between each word. HI THIS IS ELLA. Grandpa smiled big. He read it out loud, word by word. "You did it," he said. Ella held her paper up to the cloudy window and said, "Read it one more time."

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
story:
Maeva held a small clay lamp in her hands. "It is called a diya," Mama said. It was the festival of Diwali, and the street was full of people. There were sweets, drums, and bright paper flags.

Maeva wanted the diyas to shine, but hers was dark inside. "Why won't my lamp glow?" she asked. "The flame has to come from somewhere," Mama said. Mama used a match, because matches are for grown-ups. She touched the little flame to Maeva's diya. A soft light grew.

Maeva set the diya down in a slow, careful line with the others. One by one, each lit diya helped light the next. The whole row began to glow. "Now the street is smiling," said Maeva. She slipped her hand into Mama's warm hand and watched the little flames flicker.

activity: to name the five senses and say which body part is used for each
story:
Luka sat on the park bench with his grandma. Grandma had a little bag of snacks.

"Let's play a game," said Grandma. "We have five senses. Can you name one?"

"Eyes!" said Luka. He pointed at his eyes. "I see with my eyes."

"Yes," said Grandma. "I see that big rainbow kite." Luka looked up. The kite flew high.

"Next one?" asked Luka. "Ears! I hear with my ears." A dog barked. Luka heard it.

Then Grandma opened her bag. She cut a strawberry with her safe little knife. She gave Luka a tiny piece. Luka put it in his mouth. He did not chew yet. It tasted sweet.

"Now try this," said Grandma. She gave him a small slice of lemon. Luka tasted it. His mouth went tight. "Sour!" he said. "It is sour!"

"Which body part tasted it?" asked Grandma.

Luka stuck out his tongue. "My tongue! We taste with our tongue."

"That's right," said Grandma. She clapped.

Luka ate the sweet strawberry next. Then he touched the bench. It felt hard and warm. "Hands!" he said. "I touch with my hands." He smelled the lemon peel. "And my nose smells it!"

Grandma laughed. "You did it. All five senses."

Luka jumped off the bench. "Nose, tongue, eyes, ears, hands!" he sang. Then he ran to look at the rainbow kite again.

activity: simple object categories such as animals, toys and foods
story:
Athena went to the park with Dad. Under a big tree, she set out her toy cars. "Red car, blue car, green car," she said. Then she saw something yellow. It was long and round at the ends. It was a banana! The banana sat right in the row of cars.

"You are the odd one out," Athena told the banana. Dad smiled. "Yes, the odd one out is the thing that does not belong," he said. Athena put the banana in the picnic basket with the apples and the bread. Now the cars were all cars again.

Athena let her round red balloon float up above the tree. It bobbed in the wind. Then she sat down and shared the banana with Dad, slice by slice. "Goodbye, odd one," she whispered. "You belong with us."

activity: to turn on a tablet, open a drawing app and put it away when done
story:
Abigail wanted to draw a big round sun. She sat at the little table and looked at the tablet. The screen was dark. She tapped the dark screen with her finger. Nothing happened. She tapped it again and again. The screen stayed dark.

Her teacher, Miss Kim, came over. "Press this little button," Miss Kim said. Abigail pressed the button. The screen lit up. It was bright and full of colors. Abigail smiled. She tapped the drawing app and drew a big round sun. Then she drew a bird. She gave it wings so it could fly.

A boy named Sam sat down next to her. His screen was dark too. He tapped it and tapped it. "Press your button," Abigail said. Sam pressed his button. His screen lit up. "You did it," Abigail said. When they were done, Miss Kim helped them put the tablets away. "All done," said Abigail, and she patted the tablet gently, like a sleepy pet.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: common daily routines such as eating, sleeping, bathing and getting dressed
story:
Penelope loved water day at daycare. She splashed in the little tub. Splash, splash! Now her arms were wet. Now her dress was wet. Even her hair was wet. Drip, drip, drip went the water on the floor.

Max ran past her. He was dripping too. "Look, I am a wet dog!" he said. He shook like a puppy. Water flew everywhere. Miss Ana laughed. "You two need towels," she said.

Penelope wanted to go color at the table. But she was too wet. Her paper would get soggy. Then Miss Ana held out a big blue towel. Penelope rubbed her arms. Rub, rub. The towel made her arms dry! She rubbed her legs too. Now her dress was not dripping. Max came back for a towel as well. "Warm and dry," he said.

Penelope sat down at the table. She picked up a red crayon. Max sat next to her. "That was a kind towel," he said. Penelope giggled and began to color a big red apple.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: starting the first day of school
story:
Charlie stood at the gate. It was her first day of school. The playground was big. Kids ran and laughed. Charlie held her red bag tight.

A boy hopped like a silly frog. A girl found a worm by the fence. Charlie wanted to play too. But then her tummy felt funny. She needed the bathroom. She did not know where it was.

She looked around. She waited. She looked some more. The sun was warm. Her ice pop from home began to melt in her hand. She still did not know where to go.

Then she saw the teacher. The teacher smiled. Charlie walked over slowly. "Can you help me find the bathroom?" she asked. "Yes, I can," said the teacher. "Come with me." The teacher held her hand. They walked together. Charlie felt better already.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: basic color words such as red, blue, yellow and green
story:
Felix sat at the paint table at school. He wanted to make a card for Grandma. It would have one big flower on it. A pink flower, like the fairy flowers in his dreams.

But there was no pink paint. Felix looked in the cup. Red paint. Blue paint. Yellow paint. Green paint. No pink anywhere. "No pink," he said. His tummy felt a little scared. Would Grandma still like a red flower?

Miss Pia came over. "What is wrong?" she asked. "No pink," said Felix. "I need pink for Grandma." Miss Pia smiled. "Try the white paint," she said.

Felix dipped his brush in the red. He painted a big red dot. Then he dipped his brush in the white. He stirred and stirred. "Stir, stir, stir," he said. The red dot grew soft and pale. It was pink! Real pink! "Pink!" shouted Felix. "Pink, pink, pink!"

He painted a big pink flower on the card. Then he added a green stem and a yellow sun. He hoped Grandma would love it. At pick-up time, Felix held the card up high. "Look, Grandma! A pink flower, just for you!"

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: simple object categories such as animals, toys and foods
story:
Ava sat in her car seat. Mom was driving to Grandma's house. Ava had two bags. One bag held her toys. One bag held her clothes.

Ava looked out the window. She saw cows in a field. "Cows are animals," she said. "Yes," said Mom. "Just like the ducks we saw."

Ava was hungry. Mom gave her a banana from the food bag. Bananas, crackers and juice were all foods.

Then Ava looked in her toy bag. She found something soft. It was a sock! Ava laughed. She held it up. "A sock is not a toy," she said.

"That's right," said Mom. "Shirts, socks and hats are all clothes."

Ava put the sock in the clothes bag. Then she found her teddy bear. Teddy could sleep on the soft sock.

At Grandma's house, Grandma gave Mom money for the food bags. "Thank you, you are so kind," Mom said. Ava carried her teddy inside. The sock was under teddy's arm, like a little blanket.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: hosting a grandparent who comes to stay for a week
story:
Gianna stood at the big window. She watched the planes come in. One plane, two planes, three planes. Mom held her hand tight.

A door opened. Out came Grandma with her little blue bag. Gianna ran to her. Grandma hugged her and Mom at the same time.

"Wait," said Gianna. "Grandma, you hugged Mom too. Why?"

Mom smiled. "Grandma is my mom."

Gianna's eyes got big. Grandma was a mom too? "Grandma is Mom's mom?" she asked.

"Yes," said Mom. "A grandma is a parent of your mom or your dad."

Gianna thought about that. "So Grandpa is Dad's dad?"

"He is," said Grandma. "You are a smart fish."

Gianna giggled. She had one more question. "Grandma, do you make pancakes?"

"I do," said Grandma. "All week long."

Gianna counted on her fingers. One day, two days, all the way to seven. Grandma would stay for seven days!

They walked to the car. Gianna held one hand of each of them, Mom's hand and Grandma's hand, all the way.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: to put on a coat and zip it up by themselves
story:
Elizabeth had a new coat. It had big red buttons. Her old coat had a zipper, but this one did not.

At school, Elizabeth tried to zip it. She pulled and pulled. Nothing happened. There was no zipper at all.

Her teacher knelt down. "Look," she said. She held the coat open. Little holes ran down the front.

Elizabeth pushed the first button. It went right through its hole. The coat closed a little bit. She pushed the next button. Click, through the hole. The coat closed some more.

"Fast buttons!" said her friend Tom. He laughed and showed his tooth, the one that was wiggly.

One by one, every button went through its hole. The coat was all closed. It was warm and snug.

Elizabeth ran to the mirror. "I did it," she said. "All by myself."
